note: Written to be spoken: one idea per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said, never as digits. Tool and flag names are spoken as their job, not their symbol. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step. Opens on the chapter bridge line and closes on the handoff line.

lines: Everything so far has climbed one row at a time.
Now: counting positions, and picking exactly one winner when several rows tie for first.
Three different ways to count a row's position in line, and they only disagree about one thing: what happens at a tie.
One gives every row its own distinct spot, tie or no tie, no matter what.
One lets tied rows share a spot, and then jumps the count ahead by however many just tied.
One lets tied rows share a spot too, but never jumps... the next distinct spot is always just one more.
None of the three is the correct one, in the abstract. Which one is right depends entirely on what you're about to do with the number.
Here's the sharper trap, and it's a quiet one.
Say two rows tie, and you assign the first one position one, the second position two.
Run the exact same query again, same data, nothing changed. Does the engine promise to hand out those two positions in the same order a second time?
answer: No. Not unless you forced it to.
A tie leaves the order of the tied rows completely up to however they happened to come out of the earlier steps... and that can shift.
The fix costs you nothing: add one more thing to sort by, something that can never repeat, just to settle every tie for good.
Do that, and the same query, on the same data, gives you the same answer, every single time, forever.

lines: Now, something that looks obvious but quietly fails.
You try to filter directly on one of these position numbers, in the same place you'd normally filter rows.
Does that work?
answer: No. That filter runs before the position was ever computed.
Some engines give you a dedicated word for filtering after the position exists... a shortcut for exactly this.
It's genuinely convenient where it exists. It just isn't everywhere. Where it's missing, you stage it: compute the position first, filter one level up.

lines: And one last choice worth making on purpose, not by habit.
Want the top few from every single group? There are two completely different ways to get there.
One re-sorts each group on its own, over and over, once per group.
The other sorts everything once, hands out one position number to every row, and only afterward throws away whatever didn't make the cut.
Neither one wins every time. It depends on what else the data already has going for it.
So: three ways to count a tie, each one answering a slightly different question.
An incomplete order means an unreliable answer, and the fix is one extra, never-repeating column.
Filtering on a position needs that position to already exist, one way or another.
Rows arrive scattered across time. Next: pulling them back together into one coherent story.
